title: A straight-growing spicule confined to a cell surface grows along a geodetic

fields.label: Label
fields.value: A straight-growing spicule confined to a cell surface grows along a geodetic

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: A spicule tending to grow in a straight line but confined within or against a cell wall grows along a geodetic of the cell surface, so in a spherical or ellipsoidal cell it becomes a circular arc, an elliptic arc or, most often, a portion of a spiral in space, as in C- and S-shaped sponge spicules.

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: spicule follows a geodesic of the cell surface: \kappa_g = 0

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: let us suppose that it is confined either within a cell-wall or in adhesion thereto; it at once follows that its line of growth will be simply a geodetic to the surface of the cell.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter IX, “On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons”; topic “Spicules confined to a cell surface”. Scope: small curved intracellular spicules of sponges and holothurians (sigmata, amphidiscs and similar)

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: spicule follows a geodesic of the cell surface: \kappa_g = 0

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch09-08: needs-new-data, resolvability 0.52

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Geodesicity has an explicit geometric test. Existing archives may contain spicule ultrastructure, but likely lack simultaneous high-resolution cell-surface reconstructions needed to resolve the mechanism.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Reconstruct the contemporaneous cell surface and spicule centerline in 3D, then test whether the centerline has near-zero geodesic curvature and fits the shortest surface path better than unconstrained growth models. Multiple developmental stages would test the proposed confinement mechanism.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Matched developmental 3D images are rare.

Adult spicules do not preserve the cell surface that constrained growth.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.7
operationalizability: 0.85
data existence: 0.35
analysis feasibility: 0.5
data adequacy: 0.25

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: A geodesic on a stated surface is a sharp geometric prediction, and C- and S-shaped spicules can be digitized from existing images. What is missing is the cell at the time of growth, so the test becomes a fit to an assumed ellipsoid rather than a measured confinement. That proxy can reject gross mismatches and cannot separate a true geodesic from other curves that also look like circular or spiral arcs.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Reconstruct the spicule axis and test whether geodesic curvature on a spherical or ellipsoidal cell surface is indistinguishable from zero, predicting circular, elliptic or helical arcs. Systematic departure from a surface geodesic, or a fit only after implausible cell shapes are assumed, would refute the confinement rule.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The cell surface that confined growth is almost never preserved with the finished spicule.

Many published figures are drawings, and 2D projections underdetermine a space curve.
